utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you follow the proceedings in a language you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, it's Joanna Korner, Julian Nicholls, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you. Appearances for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. David Cunningham, Barbara Baruch, and Vesna Anic assisting the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank and good morning to you, too. Any preliminaries before we bring in the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do have a couple of matters to raise but I think they can wait until after the witness is concluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. May I draw your attention, Ms. Korner and the Defence team as well to a decision given by Trial Chamber II in the Stakic case on the 16th of May?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was one of the matters I was going to raise, but I can do that very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not sure that it was actually copied to the Defence in Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact it wasn't copied to the Defence, and this is one of the reasons why I'm raising it in open court so that they become aware of it if they are not already aware of it. Because it does have a bearing in one way or more with regard to the protective measures that may need to be put in place regarding the military expert.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I spoke to Judge Schomburg's legal officer yesterday who asked whether it should be copied to the Defence and I said it should. So they should be getting it at -- the Defence in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, all we would simply ask is: As Your Honour rightly says we have under the rules we had to apply for the variation in protective measures to the Stakic Trial Chamber. They in summary have said: We don't mind, that it's up to you the judges of this Trial Chamber what protective measures you impose. Your Honour, we withdrew our original filing because we were told we had to go back to the Stakic Trial Chamber. If Your Honour wants, we can refile that because the variation we are asking for is indicated in that, but I imagine that the Defence of Brdjanin must have had the original filing in any event. All I'd ask is that Your Honours make a decision, without us having to refile, unless Your Honours feel it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if it has been withdrawn, Ms. Korner, how can I reactivate it? You'll have to file it again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. We will refile it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a very simple procedure, but technically it has been withdrawn so it's not before us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. We'll refile this afternoon or this morning, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that's number 1. Number 2, Ms. Korner probably you are aware there is Mr. Ackerman's response or the Defence response to your 92 bis motion regarding Bosanski Petrovac, and also the Defence is raising objections to the various Bosanski Petrovac exhibits that reference was made to yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do want to raise that response. I have a little bit to say about it and how it impacts on the next witness. But it may well be this will take a little longer, so I wonder if we could leave it to the end of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's bring the witness. Anything from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. So let's bring the witness in. And usual precautions, Madam Registrar, while he walks in, to make sure exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before we proceed, may I ask you to repeat the solemn declaration that you made yesterday, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please be seated. Madam Baruch?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: May the witness have Exhibit P1800 in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I'd like to clear up something about this exhibit. Perhaps you haven't testified about it but it's relevant to other testimony in this case. I want to see if you agree with me with regard to the items on this exhibit, which unfortunately I do not have in my own language. That's why I need your analysis of it. Could you briefly look through the sentences in this exhibit, and I can point out some of the particular ones, item 5, which I think is on the second page -- I'm sorry, item 7 on the second page. I'm trying to establish, Mr. Witness, that everybody in this list of convictions did not get the same sentence and everybody did not get the maximum sentence. So we'll just review a few of them. Item number 7, that person only was given a fine; is that correct? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Thank you. And I apologise but I have to ask you that because we weren't provided it in my language. And he was -- person number 7, he was convicted of the same offence, that is listed next to your name, one of the later numbers, I think number 34, is that -- do you agree he was convicted of the same thing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. This is the first time that I'm seeing this, and seeing the conviction of this person. I don't know who was convicted for what reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Well, then, let's go through it a little more slowly. Item number 7 where it says "Bog" --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I interrupt for a moment? To save time, Your Honours, if this is an important document, we will arrange for it to be translated so that everybody can see what everybody got, rather than spending time with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can even save time in another manner. I mean I appreciate what you have just stated, Ms. Korner, but let me take over for a minute or two, Madam Baruch, and I will put a question to the witness Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. myself, because I presume this is the -- ultimately the question that you are meaning to put to the witness. Witness, having gone through this document, it appears obvious that there were several other persons charged and found guilty of exactly the same crime, criminal offence, as you were. That is possession of a firearm, illegal possession of a firearm or of explosives. The thing is that you got three years, according to this decision in 1994, while it seems that others got away with a different sentence. Some of them for imprisonment but much shorter than yours, for a shorter period than yours. Others by even a fine, just a fine. Do you have an explanation for that? Can you tell us why you think you got three years and others got less? Is that -- is it where you were --

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Not so much why but just that he agrees that everybody did not get the maximum sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I'm putting it to him because it appears from the document itself even if you don't know the language, and by now I have learned a little bit the language.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Me too, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. So can you give us an explanation? Why were you sentenced for three years, if we are talking of that rifle that you even doubted whether you needed a permit for, and others got a fine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't give an explanation. I don't know what this is about. This is the first time I'm seeing this document, and hearing of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just raise one other matter? It was put that three years was the maximum sentence. From what is that obtained?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I'm just -- in response, Your Honour, he got a three year sentence but others - I think he will agree - got as little as fines or just a few days, 18 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The point that Ms. Korner is making is that it seems that you said not so much why but just that he agrees that everybody did not get the maximum sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that --

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: That's all I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The source on which you're relying that three years is the maximum?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I don't pretend to even know the maximum, Your Honour but I know at least that for my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So do you have an explanation why you were sentenced to three years and others got much less than you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't, because I don't know about this. If I knew, I would have given you an explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: So with the agreement that this document will be provided in English to everybody, I need not ask you any more questions about this, Mr. Witness. My client, Mr. Witness, my client, who speaks your language, says that yesterday an interpreter erroneously translated one of your answers. So I would like some help from you in clearing up whether or not there was a mistake, and here is what the question is about. I asked you if later on, when you were in detention, you learned about other people who had rifles or weapons in Lisnja at the time that weapons were supposed to be turned in, and it was translated: I said did anybody give you that information, not question you about it but give you information, that is your other detainees? And the answer that I got in English is: "Well, when talking between each other, we would hear that because all of us were together." Now my question to you is this: My client said your response was: "Some people said they had weapons and some people said they did not." Is that your answer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recollect now what I said yesterday, whether I said it this way or that way. There were stories to the effect that there had been weapons and that there had not been weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. That's what I wanted to clear up. Now, in your statement --

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps we need to go into closed session because I want to talk about his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: So, Mr. Witness, did you spend a lot of time watching these political programmes from Serb -- on Serb television?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. On average, depends.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Well, you just said "on average." How often would you watch political programmes on Serb television in a week? Or didn't it interest you much?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, I can't give you a period of time since I don't know it. I can't tell you what I watched last month, let alone what I watched ten years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move to another topic, Madam Baruch.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: In your statement, Mr. Witness, you talked about the Muslim representatives from the village of Lisnja passing on the order to surrender guns two times. Who were the Muslim representatives from the village of Lisnja, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that it was conveyed on the first occasion. On the second occasion I wasn't there so I don't know. At the time, Gvozdjar, Enver, and Mirsad Pekic, I think were the contact persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Were those the only two Muslim representatives to the Prnjavor assembly from Lisnja?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. You said yesterday that the relationship between Lisnja and the authorities was good. Did you need any special permits to travel out of Lisnja in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean? To go abroad?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: No. I mean to travel within Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when it started, but one needed permits to go to Banja Luka. Not for Prnjavor, but if you wanted to go to Banja Luka you needed to obtain certain permits.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Did you ever obtain such a permit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I did not, because in the beginning, one could still Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. travel in a normal way and later on they introduced permits.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And everybody needed a permit to go as far as Banja Luka; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. Most probably everybody needed it because there were some checkpoints along the way.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Do you know where those checkpoints were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that they were somewhere in Klasnice.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Was there a checkpoint in Lisnja?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I have a question about the patches on the uniform of some of the soldiers you saw. I think you described them or agreed with Ms. Korner that it was something about white eagles. When did you see patches that would tell you the soldiers were white eagles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the soldiers were on the truck, one could see the insignia, and the story going around was that those were the eagles. That was the first and the last time that I came across them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. So would it be correct, Mr. Witness, that in fact you couldn't get a very clear view of the patches on the truck that just drove through, but later on somebody told you that they were eagles? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could see the patches, not quite well, because the truck was on the move. However, the story going around was that they were eagles and that's what they were shouting as they drove.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: What did they shout as they went?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were shouting, "We came to kill you, we are going to kill you. This is a Serb state." And things like that, along those lines. But I would like to point out once again that they didn't harm anybody. They simply passed through.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I understand that they didn't harm everybody. You made that quite clear. And I think you've also just clarified that you didn't really get a good look at their patches. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that I saw some patches. I think they were white and of a certain shape. I'm not very familiar with those patches but that's when I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I understand that you saw patches, they were white and a certain shape, and you aren't familiar with them. Did you conclude that this unit or this division was -- these soldiers were from the white eagles because that was the rumour in the village, that's what the villagers or someone told you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps, because there was a comment and that was concluded.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: You said yesterday that a patrol came looking for you, and for others, and suggested or indicated that you decided with someone else that he would not go to the SUP office with you and that he was SDS. Who was that person? I'm sorry, SDA.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was Rahimic, Osman, I think is his first name.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Osman Rahimic went with you -- was talking with you before you went over to the SUP station? The man that we talked about yesterday who had been hiding in the woods for some days? That man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That very man.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: By the way, have you ever seen a written statement or has anybody talked to you about a written statement by Mr. Rahimic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Have you seen any videotapes or statements by anyone other than yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: You said you were a SDA member when you were in Germany. Can you tell me what one did to become a member of the SDA? Did you pay dues? Did you sign some kind of a membership application? How did you become a member?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just like with any other party. One becomes a member, pays membership dues, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Do you remember when and where you paid your membership dues?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I paid my dues in Cologne in Germany, but when, I couldn't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Before you actually paid dues to become a member, had you ever attended a SDA meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, not really. I don't believe I did. We socialised, got together in Germany.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. What year was this, sir? When you became a member of the SDA in Germany? What year are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I arrived in Germany - I don't exactly know which month - but that was in 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm establishing this because then you can regulate more or less your questions as to relevancy, because if we are talking about 1993, in order to proceed with the questions on his SDA membership, we need to tie it up with the events that happened before or significant events that happened later that have a connection with the previous events in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I think yesterday you said that you had driven a SDA member to Sarajevo when you went to visit one of your relatives there, before your detention. Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that. I didn't take him there as a SDA member. It's just that I went to Sarajevo myself and he asked me if he could come along and I said yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And was that in the year 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think it was before that, because in 1992, one couldn't pass through to Sarajevo. That was way back while the roads were still open and passable, when people moved around normally.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Would that have been the case in 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And so you said we would socialise and get together. Did many of the people that you socialised with and got together with, were they members of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: How would I know? It's a private matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I would imagine, Mr. Witness, that since the multi-party system was rather new in the former Yugoslavia at that time that many people would talk about political affiliations. Did you never do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I was never very active in party policies.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: You said party policies or did you mean politics?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Probably it's the translation, a translation error because it's party politics that we talk of.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Do you agree with that, Mr. Witness? And this Mujanic that you saw at the police station, what was his name, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mujanic. I think his first name was Semijad or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. And you saw his name on the exhibit, right? The one that we looked at before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. Who told you that your wife had turned in the rifle to the authorities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when we talked in the culture centre, my wife told me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Oh, so you didn't know until she told you at the culture centre that she had actually turned the gun in; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I naturally didn't know. I didn't know anything since I was absent.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. So then just so that I understand something. You said when you went to the police station on Monday, you were interrogated and you were interrogated in SUP and later moved over to -- I think you were interrogated, sorry, in MUP and then later moved over to the SUP cells. At that point, you didn't know that your wife turned the gun in; is that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't even know that there was a request to surrender weapons. I didn't know anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. So then when the police were questioning you, I think you said his name was Dragan Mehtic, was he asking you about your having any weapons at that time, before you went to the cultural centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since that was -- that went on quite briefly, he didn't really ask me anything. He just asked me what the situation was like in Lisnja and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: So Dragan Mehtic at the police station, before you went to the Dom Kultura never asked you about guns; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that wasn't really an interrogation. They left me standing there alone all by myself to wait.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I think there were about two days time before you went to the cultural centre. That whole time you were just waiting, not interrogated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It wasn't two days. I spent one day sitting in an office and then the second day, or I don't know whether it was during the night or during the day, they transferred me to a cell.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And until you went to the cultural centre, nobody questioned you about guns? That's your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Nobody asked me anything in the cell.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Or at the police station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I'm going to change the topic now. I want to talk about Mr. Milankovic. You recall that you said that you saw him at the Dom Kultura?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And at that time, he was wearing civilian clothes but you recognised him because you had seen him before in Knin; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: You didn't recognise him at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the problem is he never mentioned the Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: So did you recognise Mr. Milankovic from some place else that you had seen him, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Mr. Milankovic before the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Where was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in town. I used to see him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And you told this Court that you knew that he had several convictions and was a criminal. Do you recall saying that? Before the war.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I didn't say he was a criminal. I said that he had that reputation, as an offender, somebody who had been convicted several times, and that was his deportment in general.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I was trying to find out, whether that was a reputation that other people had told you about, because my question to you, Mr. Witness, is: Isn't it true that the Milankovic, the Veljko Milankovic that you saw at the Dom Kultura was actually pretty nice and very considerate of the health and welfare of the people who were being detained? Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, his attitude was exactly what you described.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. So everything that you observed about Milankovic at that time was of someone who was making sure that detainees had food and water and could see their families and their families could bring them bedding and what they needed, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. I just was trying to make sure that we understood that what you personally observed about Mr. Milankovic was very different from what you had heard in the past. We agree about that, don't we?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And not only did Mr. Milankovic reassure you about your safety but you also said the police chief came and reassured you about the safety and the guards even told you that the conditions would be very high at the Sloga factory, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief acted in similar way as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And as time passed, the guards didn't even continue to accompany you to toilets, they let you wander around the grounds, you and the other detainees, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And all along the time that you were there, there were people who had been questioned but were being released and so conditions improved on a daily basis while you were there at Sloga; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And when you were interrogated, the people who were interrogating you, they were concerned about weapons and organised opposition to the authorities at Lisnja, those were what they were questioning about; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, topics were different. They would ask you why this, why that, what state are you living in, and there were all kinds of topics.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I'm sure that they were wanting to know something about you individually, but didn't you see the big picture of their questions was a concern about security, who was having weapons, who was organising opposition? Didn't you gather that from the questions and your conversations with other detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they asked things like, are you a member of the SDA? Are you this, are you that? The questions were non-specific. There had been no prior incidents in Prnjavor caused by people from outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Do you remember Ms. Korner saying to you: Did he ever admit to being involved in organised, armed combat? You remember she asked you that yesterday? And you said: I couldn't answer that because -- I couldn't admit to that because I wasn't present at organised, armed combat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't even know that there was any such thing. That's why I couldn't answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Yes but my question is: That's what you were being sometimes interrogated about, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Resistance, I don't know, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. You were being asked about resistance but you didn't know anything, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could I know? I wasn't there, was I?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Maybe it's the interpretation, Mr. Witness. My question doesn't go to whether you could know or couldn't know, but the questions that you were being asked, they were trying to find out about armed resistance, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that they asked me that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you said yesterday that you started your compulsory work obligation before you left Sloga. Isn't it true, Mr. Witness, that everybody was mobilised and some people refused mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about people refusing mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Well, were you mobilised? Did somebody call you up to fight?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I wasn't. The only mobilisation I had was my work obligation.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Nobody ever called you up to serve in the army? In the military?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the beginning of the war, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: From the beginning of the war until you left to Germany, no, nobody ever told you you were being mobilised? Do I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody asked me to go to the front. They only told me that I should do work obligation and I responded to that. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I'm sorry for being so confused but I heard that everybody of military -- every man of military age who was healthy was mobilised at that time. Did you ever hear anything like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Did you ever hear that Izetbegovic had announced publicly that Bosniaks should refuse mobilisation? Did you ever hear that rumour?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we identify the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't hear that either.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we identify the period that we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Prior to the time that you left for Germany, January of 1993, so we are talking about 1992 and even 1991, did you ever hear --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, no, there is a real difference between the mobilisation in 1991 and the mobilisation in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: That's fine, Ms. Korner, thank you for that. I will rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: In 1991, did you ever hear that Izetbegovic ever said Bosniaks should refuse mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And in 1992, did you ever hear, even by rumour, that Izetbegovic said that people -- Bosniaks should refuse mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. And in any event, it wouldn't have affected you because you would never have received a mobilisation order, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry, sir, I don't remember exactly how old you were but would you agree that in 1991, you were a male of military age, capable of being in the armed forces? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1990, I was seriously ill and that is probably why I wasn't called up. I have documentation proving that I was seriously ill at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I'm sorry to hear that. Can you tell me what that was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session and is it really important, Madam Baruch?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I'm trying to find out about how long it would have lasted and things of that nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you can direct the witness to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Did you ever, Mr. Witness, have any conversations or hear that there were Muslims in the Lisnja commune or Lisnja area who had very extremist views?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't say that because I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: That's fine. When we ended the session yesterday, I was referring to the place in your statement where you said that you saw people in the jail cells, that would be before you went to the Dom Kultura, whose name was Seperovic, Halilic, and if you give me a second, one other, Dzinic. And at the time you gave your statement, you said: "I can remember their given names in time." Can you tell me, I think you said it was Abdulah Seperovic. What about Dzinic? Do you remember his first name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a few Dzinics and they lived a bit further from me in a different village.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I can just direct you to where I'm getting this information. I see in the statement that you gave the Prosecutor's investigator that you said, and I'm going to quote to you, from page 3 of your statement: "As they walked me out of the cell, I walked past this cell in the same building that had bars. I could see that inside this cell were many men from Lisnja, including the family names of: Abdulah, Seperovic; Dzinic; Halilic and others. I can remember their given names in time." Now, after all of this time, since you gave your statement, do you remember who you saw in those cells by the name of Dzinic and Halilic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a few of them. I don't know who you mean. I know

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I can't help you further because I was reading from your own statement, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just interrupt? That last answer will have revealed who he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You are right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have that redacted and I'm grateful to Mr. Nicholls who actually spotted that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner. Witness, as far as possible, try not to mention relationships or names or events that would reveal you're identity.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, also at this point, I appreciate this is Ms. Baruch's first cross-examination but I am at this stage asking what the relevance of this is and whether we could move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What is the relevance of this particular question, your last question?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or last series of questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Yes. It was to tie it to the other people who had been convicted of possession of weapons and also so that we know when he talks about a person in his statement, just exactly who they are. But I'm about to leave this area, since I've assumed -- I must assume, Mr. Witness, that you cannot remember the first names of the people that you saw. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. Maybe if I saw him now, I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. And I want to go back to Sloga for a minute. Did you know or hear at the time that you were at Sloga that there were at least two Serbs detained at Sloga who had sold Bosniaks guns illegally and grenades illegally and that they were detained at Sloga during the time you were detained there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if they were. There were stories to that effect but there was not much communication between --

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. So I think we've established you didn't know to your own knowledge but you had heard that, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were stories and rumours about this person being there or that person being there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: So when you said that there were only Bosniaks at Sloga, you aren't exactly sure because you didn't know everybody who was at Sloga or what their ethnicity or background was. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know. I was not in the position to know it. It was not up to me to know everybody.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Just for purposes of what somebody else has said, would it be correct or incorrect that everybody in Prnjavor was -- everybody was wearing a military uniform in 1992? Is that correct or incorrect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say all, I don't know who you mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I'm trying to find out if everybody, all the males, at least, were wearing military uniforms in Prnjavor in 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Town or municipality?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Let's keep it as municipality, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is not clear. I don't know who you mean, men, women, where, how?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. Would it be correct that in 1992, in Prnjavor municipality, you would see men in civilian dress?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. There were men in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. And that would be true even if Prnjavor, the town? You would see men in civilian clothes; isn't that true? Yes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. And even Serb men, you saw Serb men who were wearing civilian clothes? For example, you told us Milankovic was wearing civilian clothes. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When he arrived to see us, he wore civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just trying to establish - help me here, if you can - that Serb men in Prnjavor in 1992, at least some of them were wearing civilian clothes, not everybody was wearing a military uniform, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. People who worked in the municipal building and such other places, they wore civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And even young children, even Serb young children, they would be also be wearing civilian clothes in Prnjavor, the town and the municipality? That would be correct too, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you gave your statement October 25th of 2001, which was I think about nine years after the events that you recorded, and at that time, you spoke with an investigator from the Prosecutor and there was an interpreter present. Does that comport with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of the investigator?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Would you agree that it was Paul Brady or you just have no idea?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's Grady.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Grady, I'm sorry, thank you. My typing is poor.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the name.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: That's okay. How long did you speak with Mr. Grady in October of 2001?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the exact time. We talked for a while.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Was it more than one day that you spoke with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And did you speak with an investigator from the Prosecutor on more than one occasion back in 2001?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only once.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And the next time you saw somebody from the Office of the Prosecutor was the day before you began your testimony, on Sunday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And did you -- how many statements did you give? Did you give only one written statement to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, only once, down there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And during the time that you spoke with Mr. Grady back in 2001 and also on Sunday, did anybody, Mr. Grady or any other person from the Office of the Prosecutor or any other person who was present, did they show you any documents or videotapes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I read was my own statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Did you ever contact the Office of the Prosecutor after having given your own statement to say that something in your statement was incorrect or misleading? Did you ever do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know -- what specific period do you have in mind? When I gave the statement, the statement remained the same. Now, when I have read the statement, there -- I may have come across some tiny inaccuracies.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. My question was: Since October 25th of 2001, did you ever contact the Prosecutor or attempt to contact the Prosecutor to tell them that there was something you thought needed to be changed or added to?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just make it absolutely clear so that Ms. Baruch knows, the witness doesn't keep a copy of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I was just going to ask him that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think Your Honours know the system but Ms. Baruch doesn't. The witness is not supplied with a copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Did you ever contact the Prosecutor to say that you wanted to add something to the statement that you had given them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: The reason I ask, Mr. Witness, is because there are three things that you have come to court now that -- to tell this Court about that you didn't mention at the time. October 25th of 2001. And I'm wondering if you had a full and fair opportunity to tell the Prosecutor the investigator for the Prosecutor everything that you knew with regard to the Brdjanin case back in 2001.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told them what I knew.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And they mentioned --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it was a long time ago in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. And you were told that the investigator was talking to you because of the Brdjanin case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I gave the statement, I just gave the statement about the situation in Prnjavor. I wasn't told which cases would be used in.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: You weren't told that your statement would be used in this particular case; is that right, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, we just gave our statements. There were a few of us who gave our statements. We didn't know anything. We just gave our statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Can you tell me where you gave your statement? In what facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a building, I don't know who belongs to, in Sanski Most this was, and I don't know whose building it was. It was a building, just a building, not any important building.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And did you all give your statements at the same time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They called me. I went there, gave my statement, and went on to tend to my own business.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. Witness, but you said there were a few of us who gave your statements. Did the few of you either travel together or go into the -- excuse me, or go into the waiting room together or go in and give your statements together?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was on my own when I gave my statement, and I heard that other people had also given their statement. When and how, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Were you told who the other people were who had given their statement? By anybody.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. Aside from speaking with the Prosecutor's investigator back in 2001 and on Sunday when you spoke with somebody from the Office of the Prosecutor, have you talked about your testimony with anybody else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Have you ever in your lifetime had any instruction or assistance with regard to how to testify or how to phrase your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Have you discussed what you might say here at the Tribunal with any other person besides the Office of the Prosecutor including friends or relatives or officials or representatives of any entity or organisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Have you kept any notes with regard to the incidents that occurred in 1991 and 1992, private notes, for yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't kept anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Would it be correct, Mr. Witness, because I have heard so, that in 1991 and 1992, there were frequent outages of electricity in the Lisnja-Prnjavor area, maybe even wider than that area? Was that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were outages, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And would it be correct, then, that if you watched television, when you watched television, it would have been during the day? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When there was no electricity, we couldn't watch television, and it was not that the electricity was out every night.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, while Ms. Baruch is looking can I say I did a check and it's right to say that my instructions are that the witness read through the bundle of documents from Prnjavor as well as his statement when he was here on Sunday. I want to tell Ms. Baruch that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: So, did you forget, Mr. Witness, that you did read a bunch of documents as well as your own statement - would that be correct - on Sunday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just skirmished through them, but I didn't know that you were also asking me about that. I just skimmed those documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: But, Mr. Witness, I'm asking you about every document that you reviewed prior to giving your testimony. It's quite important. So you have seen quite a few documents; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw the document about the sentencing. That's what I saw. And some orders, military orders that I saw for the first time. Whatever I saw, I saw those things for the first time in my life, and that's what I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. So any information relating to those documents, you didn't have that before you actually were shown the documents; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. The only thing I saw before that was my own statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: You said yesterday that one of the guards who had beaten up one of the detainees at Sloga was drunk at the time and came back and apologised. Do you know that guard's name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the guy very well. He is from a neighbouring village but I can't recall his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of the person he apologised for hitting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dzinic was his last name. And his nickname was Celija, but I can't remember his first name.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. Did the person who had hit you, did he apologise to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I think you said in your statement that you didn't tell any of your fellow detainees that you were hit. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Is it correct that you did not tell any of your fellow detainees that you had been hit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is correct. I didn't tell anybody.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And when you say "anybody," you mean anybody at the time, you didn't tell any other guards, you didn't tell any authorities, you didn't tell any other detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The guards were there. They were present.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: My question is whether you told -- reported it. Did you report it to any other people who hadn't been there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I didn't report it to any of the detainees, and one of the guards was present when this happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: But you didn't report it to his superior; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that he was the most superior one, the one who hit me. I don't know who it was. I don't know his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Why did you believe he was the most superior one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he came from Banja Luka. I thought that he had a higher authority, than the others, but I don't know his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I want to ask you a question about the structure. Was it always the case that the police, to your knowledge, were supervised for that region, the region of Prnjavor, were supervised from Banja Luka? From Banja Luka police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know anything about those legal structures. I really wouldn't know that. I don't know how this was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We need to stop here because we have already gone beyond the time limit that we have. We'll have a break of 25 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin is here. Let's bring the witness in, please, and we'll proceed. Yes, Mrs. Baruch.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I only have a few more questions, Mr. Witness. The compulsory work detail that you did, was that an alternative to military service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Did you know other people who refused to be mobilised who also you saw at compulsory work detail?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was there, there were perhaps some 200 or 300 people who had a work obligation, and later on, depending on the need, that number would grow. There were all kinds of people.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: After you were released from Sloga, you knew some people who weren't being detained who were in compulsory work detail, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they released us from Sloga, we rested for a day or two, and then some people were added to the group that had arrived and we started with our work obligation. We worked at two or three sites. I really don't know all the people and I don't know who worked there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Did you have conversations with your fellow workers, the people you worked with, in which perhaps one or two would say, "I refused mobilisation and that's why I'm here doing this work detail"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't discuss that. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: So you didn't speak with your fellow workers about their situation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And of course at the end of the day when you finished your work detail, you were allowed to go home and you were not under guard, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: While working, at the site where my group worked, there were no guards there. The kitchen was established and things were in order. I have to be frank about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Witness, again, you know I don't speak your language and my client says that at the end of our conversation about these soldiers that passed through your town, that had some kind of an emblem, that you said -- my client tells me that in your language, you said: "If they were or weren't white eagles, I don't know." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The story going around was that there were. Now, whether they were or were not, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what he said you said. I just wanted to get the translation correct. And just one other short area, the guard who had hit you that day, who said you lied to him, did he have any insignias or rank on a special uniform? Or was he wearing what all the guards wore?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That person was not a guard. He was an interrogator wearing civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. And everything you know about him, somebody else told you where he was from, what his position was; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I heard that he was from Banja Luka and that he came from something called DBO.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I understand that. I just wanted to make sure that that was something you heard, somebody else told you, it wasn't because of a uniform and it wasn't because this person -- this -- the man himself told you that. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't say anything, and he never wore a uniform. Always civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I pass the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Baruch. Is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just one matter, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The soldiers who drove through your village shouting at you and asking why you'd surrendered your arms, it was suggested to you that you didn't know whether or not these were Serbs or not. Can you think of any reason why Muslim soldiers would have done this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that it exists.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That what exists, I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that there was a possibility for Muslims to do that, especially in Prnjavor municipality, where there was a relatively small number of Muslims living. There were fewer Muslims there than in some other municipalities. So they really could not have organised it, the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to return just briefly to this question of why you called them white eagles. Were you able to see as they drove through your village the patches on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I could see, I can't tell you whether all of them had same patches, and on one of their arms they had something resembling an eagle with outstretched arms and there were shouts to the effect, the eagles, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The regular army, the JNA, or the TO, did they have those types of patches on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Territorial Defence had uniforms of the former JNA, the regular type of uniforms that the JNA used.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what type of uniforms were they that these men in this lorry were wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT91 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had some darker looking uniforms, multi-coloured ones, and then they had black bandanas, masks, and then gloves without fingers. So they looked different from the uniform worn by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, sir. That's all that I ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Korner, by any chance, did you intend showing the witness any photos?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So as far as Sloga factory is concerned, you stick to the diagram, the sketch that he made.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. Baruch is --

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Am I permitted to ask two follow-up questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not really, no, but if there is something extraordinarily important, sometimes we do make an exception but very rarely so.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I don't think it's extraordinarily important. I'm sure the Court can conclude the same as me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we leave it at that. And, sir, that brings us to an end. I do not have any questions to ask you. Neither do my two colleagues, Judge Janu at my right and Judge Taya. It is -- the only thing remaining for me to do before you leave this courtroom is to thank you for having come over to give your testimony. You will now be escorted out by the usher, and you will be given all the attention and -- you require, you need, to enable you to return to your country. I thank you once more.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So next --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour may I deal now because I propose to leave court with Your Honour's leave -- oh, to deal with the next witness, but can I first of all raise the exhibits produced through these witness? Exhibit P1780 was under seal which contains this witness's name. 1781 was the photograph of Milankovic. 1782, the photograph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The photograph I'm just checking Your Honour just in case -- I just want to make sure I have produced them all properly. 1782 was the photograph of the patch showing the wolf. 1783, again under seal, was the witness's sketch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And 1800, again under seal, was that criminal file which we've undertaken to get translated. And that I think is all the exhibits that were produced. May I raise the question of Mr. Ackerman's objections to the Petrovac documents and explain what I see as a problem? Can I tell Your Honour, I don't imagine Your Honours have the binder with you for Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But every document bar 2 is objected to for the reasons so-called set out in this motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, I was under the impression that this sweeping assertion that AI -- anything that came from AID was suspect or forged had gone by the board for two reasons. The first being that in the Prijedor municipality, although there were documents from AID, no objections were raised, and the second being that many of the documents from AID had been accepted by the Defence and indeed used to their advantage. Your Honour, you will recall yesterday I said this and Mr. Ackerman said no. The problem which arises is a twofold one. First, if this whole scale and sweeping objection is maintained, then in order for Your Honours to add any -- give any weight or credence to the exhibits, I have to show indicia of reliability. That I can do with the next witness who is very familiar with many of these documents but I will to have go through with him those documents, and that will take considerable time, as Your Honours know. Otherwise, I will be making a selection with some reluctance as Your Honours know because I like to read documents to the Court. Your Honour, so in any event, can I say again, not one iota of evidence has been put before the Court to show that these documents are forged. Or that documents as a class come from AID must necessarily have the stigma of a potential forgery. The second matter is this: Your Honour will recall that yesterday Mr. Ackerman had told the Court that he'd sent an e-mail saying he was missing a number of documents, and I asked if those were specified, and I was told yes. Well, we've now looked at the e-mail and, Your Honour, it is clear that if the e-mail is correct, Mr. Ackerman has been objecting to documents that he's never seen. He's just looked at the index, seen that they came from AID and objected. And not only AID these days, also from the police department at Bihac because some of the documents come from that. Your Honour, many of the documents have stamps and signatures which come from AID and to which objection is taken. Your Honour, in addition to that, there is an objection to a -- one of these news reports, the thing they used from Banja Luka Radio and there has never been any objection to that before. The objection as stated, it's P1832, is unreliable news report. And I'm not sure I follow that objection at all. The only two that are not objected to is P1813, because that was obtained from Mr. Blagojevic [phoen], the secretary to the regional assembly in Banja Luka, and then the Crisis Staff, and one which is 1841, because it was submitted by the next witness. But in actual fact, the witness submitted other ones as well, although it doesn't appear on the index, because we have used the copy we obtained from AID. Your Honour, if I may say so, I don't think, and I understand that perhaps because of the circumstances, in which Mr. Ackerman was, that he's applied his mind to this at all, and I would ask that before the witness is called, we hope sometime tomorrow, to begin, that perhaps Mr. Ackerman might reapply his mind to these objections because as I say, Your Honour, I'm extremely conscious of what Your Honour said yesterday about the time. I'm anxious not to have to waste time but it's important because these are important documents, that we establish to Your Honours' satisfaction that they are documents on which Your Honours may rely and that I will have to do if this objection is maintained. Your Honour, the other problem is raises is this: It is clear that the next witness probably won't finish today. Therefore, Mr. Hidic will not start until sometime tomorrow and then we have Thursday and then we have a Friday court maintenance. Next week, as Your Honours know, we have arranged for Mr. Kieser, who is the gentleman, the expert, from UNESCO to be here. I'm sure Your Honours will appreciate that he's a man with many, many travelling commitments because of his job and it's very important that we get him on on the Tuesday. We have a witness who is supposed to be coming next week, who equally cannot afford to be away from work for the length of time that it might be suggested. One of the problems is that VWS will only bring a witness here on Friday or on Monday. The witness is due to testify on Monday but again it looks unlikely that he's going to get on. One of the solutions would be if Your Honours were to have any influence with VWS, that they would agree to bring him here on a Sunday night so that he needn't be away from work otherwise from the Friday through until the Thursday. But, Your Honour, those are the problems. I think the most urgent one at the moment to sort out is if Mr. Ackerman can have another look at his objections to these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Baruch or Mr. Cunningham?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: If I may speak to this, I will talk to Mr. Ackerman as soon as we leave the Court and get in touch with the Prosecution to see what can be done about these exhibits, to ensure that this case moves as expeditiously as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If I may, I would suggest to you, Mr. Cunningham, that you try to do this during the next break rather than after the sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because if you can come back with some kind of a feedback from Mr. Ackerman, that can be communicated to Ms. Korner before we adjourn today, that will be better. I think you will appreciate that if we are talking of documents that the Prosecution needs to refer the next witness or the next couple of witnesses to, I mean, we need to decide on the matter by not later than tomorrow morning. Preferably, I would prefer to decide orally today, if that is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I will call him during the next break and report back to the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I appreciate that. Thank you. So next witness doesn't enjoy any protective measures, if I remember well, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So let's bring the next witness in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if Your Honours will excuse me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner, you are excused. Thank you. With regard to the other witness that you mentioned possibly bringing him on Sunday, let's talk about it again tomorrow. We should be in a better position to make an assessment of where we stand because also we have Friday, which is off this week, so that may be problematic. In that case, I will intervene tomorrow straight away with the office.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour, I'll raise the matter tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you and welcome to this Tribunal. I will be explaining a few things to you before you start giving evidence. The most important thing that we must go through, in the first place, is that you are required under our rules that before you start giving evidence you make a solemn declaration equivalent to an oath that in the course of your testimony, you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. The text is contained in a piece of paper that the usher is going to hand to you, and my request to you is to read that aloud and that will be your solemn declaration with this Tribunal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Very briefly, you're here to give evidence in this trial, which has been instituted against Radoslav Brdjanin. I am the Presiding Judge, my name is Carmel Agius. I come from Malta. I am flanked on my right by Judge Janu from the Czech Republic and on my left by Judge Taya from Japan. You will first be asked a series of questions by Mr. Nicholls, whom presumably you have met already. You have a duty to answer each and every question that he asks of you as fully and as truthfully as possible unless we stop you from answering a particular question. He will be followed by the Defence team for Mr. Brdjanin, I don't know who will be conducting the cross-examination. It will be Mrs. Baruch. And again, your duty is to answer each and every question that is forthcoming from the Defence, as truthfully and as fully as possible. You have no right to draw -- to make a distinction between answering questions coming from the Prosecution and answering questions coming from the Defence. They both have the same rights and you have just got one obligation: To answer truthfully and fully. Thank you. Mr. Nicholls, he's in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to try -- as I told you when I first met you, things move quickly in this courtroom. We are going to try to get through most of your testimony or all of it today, so please remember try to answer my questions as directly as you can while still making your answers as complete. Could you please state your name and where you were born.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: My name is Rusmir Mujanic. I was born on the 5th of January, 1962, in the village of Lisnja, Prnjavor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you are a Bosniak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you grew up in Lisnja and spent most of your life there other than your military service, and after going to school there --

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: After going to school there, you opened your own company, a logging company, which worked in the area and also in Croatia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So although you travelled around, from the time you were born up through December 1992, your home was Lisnja; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I have tried not to make objections to leading questions by the Prosecutors when they just involve preliminary matters but once we get into more important events, I'm going to object to leading questions by the Prosecutors and so I will try to -- at this point but understand that I do have general objections to leading by the Prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, they will take your objections one by one as they come along. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm going to move through this background quickly is the reason I'm doing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You were married and had a family and had your life in Lisnja up until 1992. Now, were you interested --

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In 1991, what were your main interests? Were you interested in politics?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: No. I was mostly doing agricultural work and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, did you follow political developments on the television, in newspapers, or on the radio?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: I wasn't that interested in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, did you belong to any political party in 1991 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
