utterances.text: I'd like to ask you a couple of questions about your village and your municipality that you grew up in and lived in. If I could give --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is a new map, Your Honours. I'd like to give to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do we have it or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does it have a number already?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This will be P1801.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We don't have it numbered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Presumably we don't have it, because the map that we have does have a number already. Thank you. You gave me a blank.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, could you just take a look at that map of Prnjavor municipality for a second and let me know if that looks like a reasonably fair and accurate map of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is Prnjavor actually, not Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Prnjavor, sorry if I said Prijedor. Can you please point to your village, Lisnja.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: [indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what was the ethnic composition of Lisnja? Who lived there? Was it Muslims, Serbs, Croats, other people?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Lisnja was 100 per cent Muslim village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And about how many homes were there in Lisnja? How many houses?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Around a thousand houses. I'm not in the position to give you a correct number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I'm speaking in early 1992, say January 1992, what was the population of Lisnja, your best estimate?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: I would say 20 per cent or 10 per cent, between 10 and 20 per cent had been living in Germany, working there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But in numbers of people, how many Muslims lived in Lisnja, do you think, at the end of 1991, say, beginning of 1992? If you don't know, that's okay.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number but I would say between 4.000 and 5.000, according to my estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, the village is marked in green on this map, Puraci, Mravice, Galjupovci, and Konjuhovci, are those in the correct places on the map, as far as you remember Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. Galjipoljci, for example, this is a mixed village, Serbs, Croats and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you just tell me very briefly, those villages I've just named, the other ones marked in green on this map, what was the ethnic composition of those villages? Who lived in those villages?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Mravice, for example, was a Muslim village. Konjuhovci as well. Galjipoljci was a village with mixed population. Puraci is also part of Lisnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think I'm done with that for now, if that could be entered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, briefly, when you were working and you had your company and you worked in Croatia, before the war in Croatia started, what were the relations like between Muslims and Serbs in Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: They were good. There were no problems at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What happened to your business, to your profession, after the war in Croatia started?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Because of the war in Croatia, the business simply died down. We could not work any more. We had to dismiss people, because there was just no work there any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How many employees did your company have before it was closed down?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Up to 50 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what was the ethnic makeup of your employees? Were they all of one ethnicity or different -- were Serbs and Muslims employed by you?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: There were Muslims, Serbs, even Croats. We didn't really pay any attention to the ethnicity of these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I don't expect you to remember exact dates from 10, 11, 12 years ago, but can you tell me when things began to deteriorate in relations between the Muslims and the Serbs in Prnjavor and in Lisnja?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Let's say in 1992, these relations started being tense, when the parties started promoting themselves and one could already feel the tensions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What about in 1991, in your statement you talked about a rally that you heard about. Can you tell me about that.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. In Prnjavor, there was a rally which was held by this guy Zelenbaba and he said, "Sell your cow, buy yourself a weapon." And they were singing ethnic songs and one could hear them over the loudspeakers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just to be clear, were you at this rally or did you hear about this from somebody else?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: I heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did your family remain with you all through 1992 or did they go somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: I could sense that something bad would happen, I had a premonition, so I sent my wife and my children together with my father to Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And approximately when was that that you sent them out of Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date, but in any case, it was in April.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to show the witness P82, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, I believe you looked at this -- I believe you looked at this document before you testified. This is a security services centre Banja Luka 20th of September, 1991, report on the activity of armed groups on the centre's territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Excuse me, I don't have that in -- I don't believe -- oh, yes, I do, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not going to go over this whole document, sir. I think you read pages 1 to 3 before. If you start looking at page 2 on your B/C/S version, that's the page with a footnote at the bottom of the page, footnote 1, Milankovic. That is the bottom of the first page of the attached report on the English version. Have you found that page? I can provide my page in B/C/S if that's -- all right. Now talking about armed groups on the Banja Luka security services centre territory, the paragraph in the middle of the page, in the B/C/S version, states: "Particularly characteristic is a group of about 30 armed persons from the Prnjavor area. Since 11 July, when they returned, uniformed and well armed with pistols, automatic weapons, bazookas, and grenades from training in the SAO of Krajina this group comprised initially of 25" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Baruch, I see you and Mr. Cunningham lost. We are at bottom of page 1 of the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you skip the first two pages of the document, which is a letter, and then you come to the report itself and it's the bottom -- the last paragraph on the first page.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead. And please slow down, Mr. Nicholls, because I don't want the interpreters to feel -- to have problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "This armed group comprised initially of 25 persons, mostly," and it says where they are from, "but later joined by a few other persons, has been consistently committing brazen and gross violations of law and order since their arrival, their overall activity has been complicating and exacerbating the security situation throughout the municipality and even beyond. According to intelligence gathered so far, the most extreme in these activities manifested by this group are Veljko Milankovic," and then some other persons are named. And the footnote to Mr. Milankovic states, who his father is, that he was born in 1955 in Kremna in Prnjavor and has been criminally prosecuted seven times and brought before a misdemeanour court 17 times and is the leader of the group operating in the Prnjavor area. And if we look a little further to the next paragraph, I'll paraphrase, and you can read along, that this group has been making their existence known through firing guns individually and as a group, and in villages and also at religious and other gatherings and at public meetings, where they are causing problems. The next paragraph states that this group on local and main roads at gunpoint and in a drunken state, they stop vehicles and citizens, demand to see identification papers, conducts searches, insult people, and abuse them. Finally, if we skip the next paragraph, and follow on --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We see that this group individually and as a group, they provoke and harassed the Muslim population with the aim of precipitating interethnic fighting. The centre of Prnjavor in the presence of a large number of citizens, some of them were aiming their weapons at the cars of Muslim individuals. And then it talks about shooting and harassment of the Muslim population. Does that - what I've read to you - agree with your version, the B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you were present during this time in 1991. Could you please tell the Court whether you agree with this Banja Luka security services centre assessment of the situation and problems in Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were these types of incidents, the types of incidents you were referring to in your statement where you say: "Problems were beginning to arise"?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, in what --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm done with that, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In the document we have just looked at, it talked about the -- Veljko Milankovic's group setting up checkpoints, harassing people. Can you tell me if you were aware of checkpoints being set up in 1991 in your municipality and who was manning those checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. Veljko Milankovic had the checkpoint on Vucjak. Then there was a checkpoint at the fish farm, and later on in Lisnja but yes that was later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, these other checkpoints, who was in charge of these checkpoints? If you arrived at one of those checkpoints, who was going to stop you?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: The army that belonged to Veljko Milankovic, the so-called wolves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I -- what I'm getting at is: Were there other checkpoints that were manned by anybody else, by police or military or any other groups?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: We as the TO had the right to control Muslims and others whoever, if we found that there was something suspicious. That was the authority that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, who ordered the setup of these checkpoints, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Our order arrived from Banja Luka, Captain Nedjo was showing it to us because I was also a member of the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. We will talk about the TO as a subject in a minute. So now when you're talking about checkpoints, orders from Banja Luka, you're talking just, you're talking about TO checkpoints; is that right, to be clear?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, who was -- you've just said Captain Nedjo. Who was Captain Nedjo and what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: He was a Serb, and he was a captain in the Territorial Defence of Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, these checkpoints that were set up, TO and otherwise, could Muslims, Serbs, and Croats all pass through those checkpoints without problems, or did the checkpoints apply differently to different people, did different ethnicities have more or less difficulty passing through these checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: For example, as one left Lisnja to go to -- towards Mravice, there was a checkpoint. I knew these people, they asked for IDs, if you didn't have your ID on you, then they will tell you to go back. You couldn't proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And my question is: Were these restrictions applied to people of all ethnicities equally? Was it just as hard for a Serb as a Muslim to get through one of these checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: No. This was only for Muslims, for just one ethnicity, or rather for Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you were a member of the TO; is that what you started to say a minute ago?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you remember, approximately, when were you mobilised, called up, into the TO again and issued a weapon?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Very hard for me to answer that question. It was a long time ago, but I believe it was in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: In late 1991, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And tell me just briefly about your TO unit. Was that a Lisnja unit or just for the village of Lisnja or did it encompass a wider area?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: It was the Territorial Defence of Lisnja village but there were also five Serbs from neighbouring village, so it was a mixed TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. If there were five Serbs from a neighbouring village, how many Muslim TO members were there from Lisnja?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: There were around 40 of us altogether, I should think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And were you issued a weapon once you were called up of mobilised as a Lisnja TO member?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had a machine gun. There were two machine guns in the village and there were also M48 rifles with 30 bullets each and my machine gun had 150 bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And briefly can you tell us what a M48 rifle is, what kind of rifle is that?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Those are old rifles, God knows how old they were. Some of them were even out of order, out of the 30 that we had, maybe half of them were in a proper working order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And just briefly, can you tell the Chamber about what your duties were as a TO member at that time? What activities did you engage in as a TO member?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: We made sure that there were no unrests in the village, or if somebody carried illegal weapons, we had the authority to take them away. So we made sure that nobody created any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just one question: Why -- was it normal or did it seem surprising to you that there were five Serbs from a neighbouring village in your TO Lisnja unit?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I found it normal. I did not make any distinctions at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you stated in your statement that in around March of 1992, the problems really started. Can you tell us what you meant by that, what kind of problems started or escalated in and around March?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: We were patrolling during the night, it was in Puraci. We were on the main road. We could hear gunfire. There were tracer bullets to be seen. And we could hear singing and then there was the other exit towards Glavica [phoen] which is another Serbian village. There one could see the inscription on the asphalt, this is Serbian land, and one could see and witness all sorts of provocations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You said you could hear singing. Can you be a little more specific about why you -- what kind of singing that was or why it would bother you or create apprehension in you?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: For example, there was gunfire and there were -- the songs, the words were, "You are a goner, Alija," Alija being a synonym for a Muslim. And then there were other words saying, go away to Turkey; in other words this meant -- well, this is a Serbian land, and there is no room for you here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were there any problems other than that with other shooting events or with people driving in Lisnja shooting? Can you describe any other events that you experienced?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the main road between Banja Luka and Prnjavor and Derventa, as lorries would pass by, probably carrying ammunition, they were escorted by combat helicopters, there were troops there, and they would shoot towards the houses and they didn't even think twice whether there was maybe somebody in those houses, they would break the glass on the windows of these houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, specifically, you said lorries and carrying ammunition. Which -- do you know which soldiers these were or who these people were?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: That was the army, I don't know. The Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And as a TO member, did you report these incidents or try to do anything about them?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We reported to Captain Nedjo but nobody reacted to that and nobody tried to prevent these things, and we ourselves didn't dare do anything on our own.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Why didn't you just -- we can move on, but why didn't you dare as a TO member to do something on your own? I mean, there were 40-odd members and you had some arms.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: If somebody came to attack us, how would we have defended ourselves? The weapons we had were no weapons at all. We were a minority there, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to move on to another topic, also about weapons. At any time were the people of Lisnja called upon to surrender their weapons? I'm not talking just about the TO.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a meeting and the security captain was there, Captain Nedjo was there, and also there was a guy from Banja Luka, an officer, I don't know who he was exactly, and there were three of our representatives there, and we were required to hand over our hunting rifles. And they gave us two or three days deadline to do it, and then we did it and we took all these weapons to Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, how did you -- if you remember, how did you find out about this order to turn over hunting rifles? Was this communicated by the police, by the military, by civilian authorities, or was it just something you heard from a neighbour? How did you find out about this requirement?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Well, there was this meeting and our representatives were there, there was somebody from Banja Luka, there was a security officer, there was Captain Nedjo there, with the police of course, and the police informed us -- actually it was our representatives who informed us about this requirement to turn over the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Just for clarity, were you present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What happened to the two machine guns which had been issued to the TO -- to your TO unit?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Captain Nedjo came and he said they are needed at the battlefield since there was a shortage of weapons and we had to surrender them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what about the M48 rifles?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: They remained until the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You were never specifically asked to turn that in?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, from what you heard about this meeting and the request to -- or the order to turn in weapons, can you just tell us a little bit about what your representatives told you about how urgent this was? I mean, was this sort of an optional activity that there was a request that you could turn in weapons or were any threats made if this order wasn't complied with? Tell us what the feeling in the community was when you heard about this requirement to turn over hunting rifles.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: We resigned ourselves to that. We knew what would happen if we failed to surrender. Everybody had a good thought and decided that they had to surrender weapons, and if we didn't surrender them, we know what would have happened. They would have killed us because they already started surrounding Lisnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Who is "they" when you say "they" in that answer you just gave?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: I mean the Serbs, police and the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Who had started surrounding Lisnja at this time when there was an order that the weapons be turned in?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: There were troops there, soldiers, with the SAO Krajina insignia and the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you said there was a deadline. Were there any threats made of what would happen if the weapons were turned in? You said you thought you knew the people thought they knew that they would be killed but were any threats specifically made about what would happen if the weapons were not surrendered?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Well, they said in order to avoid major consequences, it is better to surrender weapons in order to avoid any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. So there was sort of a promise that there would be peace and there wouldn't be problems if you did surrender the weapons? Did I understand you?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, if you know, did this surrender of weapons apply to all ethnicities equally? Were Serb villages being disarmed at this time?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: No. Just Muslims, non-Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, how do you know that? What's your basis for knowing that, if you could explain, please?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: I can say that because Mravice also had to surrender weapons. Only Muslims had to, as did Konjuhovci, Galjupovci, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, were weapons in fact surrendered based on this order? And did you personally surrender any weapons, if you could answer both those questions.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have a brother-in-law working abroad, so I had two hunting riffles, a sniper, and another weapon, and I surrendered that immediately. I took that to the police, and a neighbour took us in a truck there. In fact, he loaded us all in the truck and we went there and surrendered that to police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Which police station was this? In which town?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: In Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And to whom did you physically surrender these guns? Can you sort of describe the process? Were people lining up or were names called out? What actually happened when you surrendered these weapons?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: No. We were lined up in a row, carrying our weapons and as we got there, we approached two policemen and as we surrendered the weapons, they issued receipts to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How many people did you see there surrendering weapons at the same time that you surrendered yours? Was there a lot of people there or just a few or --

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Some people surrendered earlier. We had a three -- two- or three-day deadline, so whenever people had time, they went into surrender. We went in a group of perhaps 30 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Besides the police who were present, was anybody else present supervising the surrender of weapons?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were soldiers there. I know that they had SAO Krajina inscription on it. They cursed our mothers, they said: "Here you are surrendering weapons. We are going to kill you." And so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How many soldiers were there when you surrendered your weapons, your brother-in-law's weapons?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: I had my brother-in-law's weapons there. There were two trucks there as well but we couldn't really look around because we knew that there were quite tense, they were cursing us, cursing our mothers. We knew that they were ready to kill us. That was their desire. They sort of were there and were saying: "I hope -- we hope we did not come in vain."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, were these soldiers, did they appear to be just there or were they taking part in the process, helping the police, in the taking of these weapons?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: They were invited to come there and we concluded that based on the fact that they said to us: "We hope we didn't come in vain," that means that they had been invited.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, to your knowledge, did anybody from Lisnja refuse to surrender their weapons and were there any further calls from the authorities demanding that weapons be surrendered?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Nobody refused to obey. Everybody surrendered their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Maybe I'm not being completely clear. You spoke in your statement about some groups, two groups of men who took some weapons and ran off. So I guess they didn't surrender them. Can you describe that, if you remember it, that incident?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Those were other weapons. People who were issued automatic weapons, then several days later, the same thing happened. They said that if we failed to surrender weapons before noon, we would be considered enemies and be killed. There was a group of people, some 20 to 30 people, who indeed had been issued those weapons without ammunition or anything else, and they left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Nicholls, Judge Janu is drawing my attention to a very important matter. Your previous question was -- contained two questions in one actually. And the witness answered only the first part of the question and not the second. The question was: "Now, to your knowledge did anybody from Lisnja refuse to surrender their weapons?" That was answered. "And were there any further calls from the authorities demanding that weapons be surrendered?" This part of the question has not been answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I apologise. That was a bad question. I think he was just getting to it talking about the automatic weapons, but I can ask that again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You responded to a call to surrender weapons and you turned over these weapons as you've told us about the process. After that, were there any other calls besides the one you responded to, to surrender weapons? You started talking about automatic weapons. Can you explain that, please.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the call to surrender people -- weapons that had been purchased by people earlier, so there was a call to surrender those weapons and there were no further calls to surrender hunting weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And now you were saying that some people did not obey that second call to surrender those weapons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. People were bringing in the weapons they had purchased. That was in the culture centre. There were the premises of the local commune there and this is where they surrendered the weapons. A group came in and they collected those weapons and they went to an elevation called Vinogradije.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That group -- just to be clear, that group that you say took the weapons and went to this area, were they Muslims or Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And before we move on, how many -- how big was this group? How many men were in this group that took the weapons?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: 20 to 30 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You served in the military for a couple years, correct, and you were a member of the TO?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was a member of the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you saw the Serb -- the regular armed forces of VRS, Milankovic's men, these other soldiers that you saw when you surrendered your weapons, and the police. What kind of resistance do you think these 10 to 20 -- these 20 men could put up against all those other forces, if they wanted to?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: No kind of resistance whatsoever. They had no ammunition to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to move on a little bit. There were these tour surrenders of weapons. Other than this one incident you talked about, people in Lisnja did surrender their weapons, that's what I understand your testimony to have been. Did that secure the peace of Lisnja? Did everything carry on peacefully after you obeyed those orders or were there further problems?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: When the weapons were surrendered, we were then surrounded from all sides, Veljko Milankovic's men were there as well, police, then there was a group from Laktasi, I know that for a fact. They surrounded the village, dug out trenches. Then they told us that we have to leave the village or else we would be considered enemies so we went down to the sawmill and all of us went down there to the sawmill.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, how long after you had surrendered your weapons did this take place, that there was this announcement that everybody had to leave Lisnja?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Immediately after the weapons were collected, people started fleeing. There was nothing else to do. Then they used a loud speaker to announce to us that we had to leave the village, whoever failed to leave the village would be considered an enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, try to -- if you can, try not to -- try to, if you can, answer my questions specifically rather than saying "they" to refer to people. That would be helpful. Who is the "they" who announced that everybody had to leave the village? Who made the announcement over these mega phones?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: That was Radivojevic, Milankovic. They said that to us in Lisnja, that we had to go down to the sawmill and if we didn't, we would be considered enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. How -- how many -- where was the sawmill in relation to the centre of Lisnja? How far away was that?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Not more than 2 and a half kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And was this order obeyed? Did the people from Lisnja leave their village?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was among the first to leave. I put women and children in my tractor's trailer and I headed towards the sawmill. There was a column of a kilometre and a half of people leaving. They couldn't go down later on in trucks, cars and other vehicles, so they just left their belongings and went down there on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The whole village?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. Some people remained who had been working the land and they didn't know about what was going on so there were very few people in that group, and another group that remained were the handicapped persons and the elderly who couldn't leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. So virtually everybody who could, left; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What happened at the sawmill when you got there and all these hundreds or thousands of people arrived?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Well, we got down there to the sawmill and we were there, fenced in by a wire. Nobody touched us there. I got rid of my uniform, as I didn't have any weapons or anything else. Then a man came from the Territorial Defence and Veljko Milankovic, and they started cursing and they collected the weapons and that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And was the whole of the village able to be kind of contained or were people spreading out? I mean, when you say "fenced in," can you describe a little more for me what -- what it was like to be there that day, after leaving your village.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Well, down there, some people were fenced in by wire and then there was a restaurant called Europa there as well, and then there was a house across the road that had a large basement and some people were in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you mentioned Veljko Milankovic, I think, was there and we've read a little bit about him. But did you know who he was before -- well, had you ever met -- did you personally see Veljko Milankovic at the sawmill?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: I didn't know him from before. Later on, I learned that that was Veljko Milankovic. I had never seen him before, nor did I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But did you personally see this man who you later learned was Veljko Milankovic, at the sawmill?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was some ten metres away from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, other than his men, who -- who was in charge of the sawmill? Who was guarding the people from Lisnja or telling people what to do? Who was in charge there?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Veljko Milankovic, Radisic. There was another officer whom I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I think we might have covered this but I don't remember if I asked you: Do you remember the name of the unit or what the name was that Veljko Milankovic's men was called?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Wolves from Vucjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Did they have any particular symbol or insignia or patch that identified members of that unit?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. They had an emblem with a wolf's head and there was an inscription underneath saying Wolves from Vucjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you see men wearing those patches when you were at the sawmill?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you said also that, if I heard you, that some more weapons were surrendered at the sawmill. Can you tell me which weapons those were? Just tell me what that was about.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Those were M48 rifles from the Territorial Defence, which nobody requested us to surrender until the last day, and then that day when Milankovic was there, all those weapons were collected. Also people who had pistols with licences, also surrendered them because that's what Milankovic and Radisic required them to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And this is a bit of a silly question, but why did you surrender? Why were these weapons surrendered on that day? Why did you agree and obey to give those weapons up to Mr. Milankovic?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: We had to surrender them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What did you think would happen if you didn't?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: They would have killed us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, how long were you personally detained at the sawmill? I take it from your description that you weren't free to leave. But tell me how long you were detained there.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Until the noon of the following day. That's exactly when they released us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And was that everybody in the village or some of the people? Was that the whole village was held for that time?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: No. A group of, I don't know how many people, around 250 to 300 people left for Prnjavor in buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: That was on the -- in the evening, they took away Senad, who had a shotgun wound in his left shoulder, whereas the other people were driven away in the morning at around 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And who were the people who were put on these buses and taken to Prnjavor? Were those men, women, children, or a mix? Can you just tell me.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Only men who were fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, what else did you observe happening at the sawmill while you were held there? Were the men and the women -- you said some men were taken away by bus. Were the men women and the children from your village allowed to mingle and stay wherever they wanted inside that area or were they separated in some way?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Well, women mostly went to the restaurant and to the house, to the rooms upstairs. So the women and children were there and in the restaurant, whereas we remained outdoor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, while you were there, did you see or hear of Veljko Milankovic directing any military operations or making any orders, not just about people who were being held there or the surrender of weapons but telling soldiers what to do?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You heard about that or -- the question was different. Did you see or hear of Veljko Milankovic directing any military operations or making any orders? You didn't see but you heard of it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I both saw and heard it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you saw it with your own eyes and you heard it with your own ears.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, you heard the -- Veljko Milankovic directing. You didn't hear of Veljko Milankovic directing, you heard Veljko Milankovic himself directing military operations. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I wasn't far from him so I could both see it and hear it as he was lining up his unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question was a little bit -- or hear of Veljko Milankovic directing. And I could see that what he was saying was not exactly in reply to your question. Or there was some kind of misunderstanding in any case. So let's proceed, Mr. Nicholls. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for clearing that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you tell me what you saw and heard him directing, that the military should do? And you referred a bit in your statement about the movement of guns or artillery, can you tell us about that, if you remember it.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. He wanted a multiple rocket launcher and recoilless gun to be brought there and to be deployed in a village near Pavlovo Brdo. So those weapons were brought in there and then they issued a half an hour ultimatum. There was a Hodza, Jusuf, there and he wanted the young men who collected the weapons to return and to surrender so that there would be no problems there. So a lot of those young men returned indeed and threw away their weapons and ammunition which they couldn't use any way. As they were coming back, there were hitting these young men with butt rifles -- rifle butts, and then Hodza returned as well, and then they started shelling Lisnja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to stop here for the time being. We will resume in 25 minutes from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: May I interrupt?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption. The Court had asked me to contact Mr. Ackerman to determine what if any changes there were in the Defence positions with respect to the objections that he filed. He indicates to me that he wishes to stand which those objections. At the end of the day, I will speak with Mr. Ackerman again, if there is any change from that position, we will contact the Office of the Prosecutor immediately and let them know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And we will wait then and we will hand down an oral decision tomorrow morning. Okay? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. One point before we move back to the testimony, the Prosecution would like, and if it's acceptable to the Court, to consider sitting a full day on Thursday. That would be 9 to 12.30 and then 2 to 4.30 and also next week, to try to get caught up. Ms. Korner has checked with VWS and they have no problems with that. I've told Mr. Cunningham about that proposal in the break and I think the Defence needs more time to think about it, but that's one idea we have to speed things along if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you're suggesting this Thursday, 9 to --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 12.30 and then a break and then 2 to 4.30 --?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 2.15, whichever the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because usually it's 2.15, especially if there is an another Chamber sitting, they -- what did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's why if it's possible it could move things along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's hear what the Defence has to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I think we need to look at the witnesses and consider that, but I do know one thing, Your Honour. My client is in a very small, uncomfortable place in the back here, without a toilet in the room, and he spends a lot of time, a lot of his time, waiting there like during our lunch hours and things like that. Would it be a different courtroom, with a different cell? Or did I understand Chuqing correctly that it would be this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If I read Ms. Chuqing correctly, she is suggesting that this courtroom, this particular courtroom, will be available throughout the whole, the entire week. That's next week.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I'm just pointing that particular problem out to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I want to know is this: When we sit in Courtroom III or in Courtroom I, is Mr. Brdjanin kept in a different room?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: When I appeared before the Court months ago, the cell area that he had was bigger, with a bathroom in it, and somewhat more comfortable. I'm not saying that a jail cell would ever be comfortable, but this one in particular is very small and no bathroom there in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And is he kept in this small cell only when we are sitting in Courtroom II?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I can't -- if you give me a chance? Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. All right. Ms. Chuqing, where is she? She is disappeared. Yes, Chuqing, we need to see first whether there is any other courtroom available for us to sit the entire day next week. I suppose --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's impossible, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's impossible. So next thing I would like is to ensure -- to see what the alternatives are, in other words, where Mr. Brdjanin could be kept so as to lessen the inconvenience as much as possible. At the same time, Mrs. Baruch, this courtroom is usually used by Trial Chamber III or Trial Chamber I, I think in another trial, one week after the other, and the accused is kept therefore in this room. I'll see what I can do. I'll see what I can do. In the meantime, do you agree that we sit on Thursday extended hours on a different time schedule and the entire of next week unless of course we have problems?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: May we please try it on Thursday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will try it on Thursday, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And with some consideration for the comfort of my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We try it on Thursday, but we then need to know because VRS would need to be put in a position where they can bring over witnesses. In other words, we will have to organise ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So Thursday, Madam Chuqing? All right? You need to make some adjustment to the Court schedule. 9 to 12.30. Then resuming at 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Whatever the Court prefers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Resuming at 2.00, up to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 4.30 is what I'm told is the suggestion but whatever fits your schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Resuming at 2.15 and stopping at 4.30. Resuming at 2.15 and stopping at 4.30, all right with you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We try first Thursday and then we see. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, I want to go back to the question we were on just before the break. I'm sorry that you had to wait through this scheduling matter that had nothing to do with you. You stated - I believe it's off the screen - that you heard and saw personally Veljko Milankovic asking or ordering that this rocket launcher and recoilless gun be moved on a hill, and I think you said they did it for him or something like that. Can you tell me who it was that Milankovic was asking to move these artillery or weapons on to this hill.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: He was talking to an officer. I don't know who he was. I don't know his name. But in any case, he was an officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: A VRS officer, is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I'm going to object to the Prosecutor leading the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where is he leading him?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Just now when the witness said "an officer," and the Prosecutor suggested the kind of officer as opposed, for example, to Mr. Milankovic's office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a perfectly legitimate question, Madam Baruch. I accept it. Go ahead. He's not leading him. It's not what a leading question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You may answer the question, if you know the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And also, Madam Baruch, the practice of this Tribunal as to leading questions, it's much, much more wide, it's much wider than it is in any domestic jurisdiction that you know. The same -- that you are familiar with, as also with my jurisdiction. Here we proceed unless it is absolutely very much undesirable to have the question put the way it is put, we don't normally stop the attorney from using leading questions. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, were you able to see whether this order was carried out? In other words, were you able to see any movement of a recoilless rocket -- of a rocket launcher or a recoilless gun?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, one other thing before the break you said that this was Veljko Milankovic and you didn't know him beforehand. How did you find out, if you remember, who told you that guy there is Veljko Milankovic or could you specifically tell us how you learned who this man was who was giving orders?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: When this order was being issued, there was a neighbour of mine, standing next to me, who knew him and he told me: Well, this is the guy, this is Veljko Milankovic. I myself had not known him before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Then you started talking about how the Hodza went to try to get some young men who had not surrendered their weapons and that these men came back. Just to be clear, is this part of the same group of people who you said took some weapons and went up into the woods or is this completely unrelated to that group of people who took the weapons and went up into the woods that you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: It is that same group of people who went up to that hill, Vinogradije and then the Hodza came to them and then they returned, they were beaten up, they were beaten by rifle butts, and then they were taken behind Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we will move along but you've said this was the village of Lisnja which was held at the sawmill. Did you see anybody you knew who was of Serb ethnicity who was a prisoner there?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a man who used to come to us, we used to receive Serb refugees and accommodate them in our houses. All the refugees were then brought and taken away, and this Serb was the only guy who remained there. He was curious to see what was going on. He says: Well, let me see what's going on? You seem to be very good people here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Other than him, were there any other of Serb ethnicity you saw being detained at the sawmill?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't see any other Serbs. He was the only Serbian person whom I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, did the people from your village who were held at the sawmill offer any resistance that you saw while you were there? Did they put up any fight against Milankovic or any of the other troops or police who were there?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: No. They didn't put up any resistance. They didn't try to fight. They wouldn't have stood a chance, even if they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And as far as you know, was there any resistance from the people who had remained in Lisnja behind who couldn't come to the sawmill?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: No. There was no resistance. They didn't have any weapons, so nobody as far as I know put up any resistance. That's as far as I know, because I was by the sawmill at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, could you actually see from your position by the sawmill, the village of Lisnja or any part of it? Can you describe what you could see of Lisnja.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: You could see 65 to 70 per cent of the village of Lisnja from the place where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'd like to go through this bit quite quickly. And I won't lead unless counsel doesn't object. But were you personally threatened by any soldier or person --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Here for the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Time being, just ask him whether he was threatened, don't suggest by whom he could have possibly been threatened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were you threatened personally in any way, directly, while you were held at the sawmill?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. A person called Tito Potok asked me to start jump the Mercedes but I couldn't do it. I don't know how to do that. So I said I would try to find somebody who could do that but I couldn't find anybody. My brother-in-law came by and said: "Try -- run away because he is looking for you to kill you. Hide amongst the women and the children." And that's what I did. I hid amongst the women and the children. I was there all night and then all the follow morning, I left that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And just to be clear, my translation says start jump this car. Does that mean -- could you describe what that means? Is that starting it with jumper cables or starting it with without a key or what does that entail?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: That means without a key. To hot wire, to use wires to ignite the -- to start the engine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, tell me whether you saw that rocket launcher and recoilless gun? Did you see that gun fire at any time while you were at the sawmill, either of those guns, sorry.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did, because that was some 100 metres away on that hilltop and one could see everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you see who anybody order that the guns be fired or did you just see them start firing?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't see that, but Milankovic issued that order. I was very close to him, and I heard him saying that he would open fire on Lisnja if those lads did not return very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And when that rocket launcher and recoilless gun did start firing, where was the fire directed to? Could you see where the target was, what was hit, if anything?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Well, the fire was opened on the village. I don't know where exactly. I know that two shells fell very close to the mosque and I know that the -- my brother-in-law's house was set on fire actually its roof was set on fire by a shell. That's what I could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. You say "the village." That's your village, Lisnja, is that right, that was being shelled?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Approximately how long did that attack last?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Some ten or so shells were fired, were launched.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just to be clear, could most of the people who were gathered there see this shelling of their village or were you in some unique position where only you could see it?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Most of the people could see that. I was not there by myself. Because there is this house and the restaurant -- and a few metres around the corner, if you're standing there, you could see everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And you started talking about it but was there anything else that you could see damaged by this shelling of Lisnja? You said some shells landed near your mosque. You talked about your brother-in-law's house. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Excuse me, I don't know if the question is directed to while he was -- while the witness was at the sawmill.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Baruch.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll ask that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: During this shelling, what buildings were you able to see or what damage could you see was caused from where you were positioned at the sawmill during the shelling?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: I saw some houses aflame, but I could not see exactly what houses those were until the following day when we were released at noon and when we went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, during this shelling of Lisnja, were you able to see any return fire from Lisnja, any kind of resistance, anything that would show you that -- that there was a response to the shelling from the village in Lisnja?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What happened after the shelling stopped? Tell us what happened next.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Veljko Milankovic lined up his troops and ordered them to launch an attack, and then troops started from the other side, there were some troops from the Laktasi area that arrived. In any case, the whole area was encircled.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. How many troops, if you can give me an estimate, did you actually see there, Veljko Milankovic's men and other armed soldiers or men?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Where we were, there was some 50, not more, men. And there were also policemen there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, did Veljko Milankovic say or do anything to protect his men while he was sending them off to attack Lisnja, as you said? Did he take any precautions?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. He took 20 hostages. I was close and I managed to hide. There were 20 hostages and among them was a Serb who volunteered, so they were -- these hostages were put in a -- in close confinement and they -- it was said that if anything should arrive to any of the soldiers, these people would be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, do you know to those people, the hostages? Were they killed or were they eventually -- or were they not killed?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: No, they were not killed. Later on, they were transferred to Prnjavor with all the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I don't know if you were or not, but were you able to see at all what Veljko Milankovic's men were doing once they entered Lisnja? Could you see that or any activity?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: No. I could not see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, what -- you spent the night at the sawmill?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the next day, I think you said around noon, you were released; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Was everybody who remained released at that time or were you released before other people?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Some two hundred and -- or thirty people were taken by buses to Prnjavor, and the rest of us were released.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And were you told anything upon your release, what to do, where to go, what was going to happen next, to the people of your village?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: They didn't say anything. Before that Radivojevic [Realtime transcript read in error missing word "Radivojevic"] said that fit men would be taken to one side and that not so fit would be taken to another side. Then he changed his mind and then he told us that we could go to the village only afternoon, after 12.00, after the mosque in Puraci had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thanks, could you say the name of the person who told you this? I don't think that was picked up on the transcript. Who told you that the fit men would be taken to one side and that the others would be placed somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: His name was Radivojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And who was he?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: I don't know what position he held in Prnjavor, but he was on the top. He also wore a uniform, a multi-coloured uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You mean camouflage?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Where did you go after -- at noon that day, when you were allowed to leave?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: I went home.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what did Lisnja look like when you arrived back home? Not just your house but the town as a whole, if you can describe what you saw.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: It was a ghost village, a lot of smoke, roofs were crumbling in, and when I came close to my house, I saw that it had been set on fire. My brother's house was intact. There was a lot of smoke. Barns had been set on fire and also livestock was burning and you could feel that terrible smell in the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were any homes still burning, still on fire?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. Some 76 houses were still burning and some outbuildings as well, and barns.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And could you tell whether any property had been stolen, if there had been any looting and was anything taken from your families' or anybody-you-know's house?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: In my brother-in-law's house, nothing was there. Everything had been taken away, couches, beds, and I heard from Osman Rahimic, he was watching everything from a forest, from a tree, and he saw neighbours, civilians, the army, taking away our property, our things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, do you know whether any civilians from Lisnja were injured or killed during the shelling and/or -- well, just during the shelling, first.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the morning, Tito Potok told us: "I had killed these guys. There they are, up there, lying." And then he ordered a group of us to go there to collect the bodies by a tractor so a few men went there and collected the bodies. And on that same evening, Avdic, Senad, who had been shot earlier on had a penetration wound in the left shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, just to be clear, did Tito Potok tell you that he'd personally killed these men or that they had been killed because I'm not 100 per cent sure from your answer. Because I asked --

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. He said that he personally had killed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, was there a mosque in Prnjavor in Puraci? I may be pronouncing that incorrectly.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: There was a mosque in Puraci, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you see anything happen to that mosque around the time you were released from the sawmill at noon?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Before noon, a tractor came by, carrying some green boxes and sometime around noon, one could hear detonation, an explosion, and then one could see the top of the mosque caving in, crumbling in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And when you went -- well, were there any mosques in Lisnja, actually in the village?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a mosque in the main street, and as I was walking by it on my return, I could also see that it was burning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to show you a photo now, P1796.1. This is a photo you were shown on Sunday. Can you tell me, if you can, it's not the best photo in the world, can you tell me what's depicted here, if you recognise this spot.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is Turbe, and this is the house of a neighbour of mine, whose name I cannot recollect now, and this is where the mosque was, right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I couldn't see it. Could you indicate again where the mosque was.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: [indicates] I think it should be somewhere here but I don't know from what direction the picture was taken. There were some remains here but they are not depicted in this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And which mosque used to be at the spot? Which of the ones that we talked about?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Mosque in Carsija, in downtown area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Of? Of which village? Of Lisnja?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I just remembered this house here belongs to Husein Pekic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I'd like to show you another photo. The next one is 1796.2. Just tell me what that is.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: These are the new foundations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Of? Just for the record, could you say what it's the foundation for?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: For the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I'm finished with that. Now, can you just tell us what was going through your mind and how you felt as you walked through the town you'd been born in that day after you were released from the sawmill and how what you saw and what had happened to you made you feel?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Well, I felt bad. All I wanted was to run away from there and forget about everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to go through just a few more documents with you, sir. P657, please. This is the 2nd of June, 1992, 1st Krajina Corps command, regular combat report. This is a document you looked at very briefly on Sunday as well, sir. If you look at the last sentence of paragraph 1, it states: "In Lisnja village, an armed conflict occurred between Muslim extremists and the army of the Serbian Republic of BH. Some of the Muslim extremists were captured while a rather large number of them pulled out towards Crni Vrh." I'm sorry for my pronunciation. Can you tell me what's true and what's not true in that sentence as somebody who was present?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Nothing is true in this sentence. First of all, they didn't go towards Crni Vrh. I know though that they did get the weapons, these 30 to 30 young men. However, there was no combat, no bullet was fired by our people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And in the last sentence of paragraph 2, which states: "In the area of Derventa there continues to be occasional artillery fire, while because Muslim extremists have failed to hand in their weapons, the Muslim population of the area of Lisnja village has been expelled." Can you comment on that sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: First of all, all of the weapons in our possession were surrendered. However, when we were in the camp, they forced us to, for example, buy weapons and then surrender them to them. However, we did not have any more weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What about the last part of the sentence, about the village of Lisnja having been expelled? Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were expelled to the sawmill. We left the village. And we returned and then again in 1995, the entire population of Lisnja was expelled again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Right now let's stay with 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to have the witness look at P659, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is a -- another 1 KK combat report, regular combat report of 3rd June, 1992. Sir, I'd like you to look at the -- again the last sentence of paragraph 2. Which states: "Measures have been taken to continue mopping up the areas of Kozarac, Prijedor, Sanski Most, Kljuc, and Lisanja [phoen] village near Prnjavor." I think that's Lisnja. On 3rd of June, 1992, after Lisnja had been shelled, who was in control of the area around Lisnja and who was militarily in control of Prnjavor? Does this statement seem true, that there was this mopping up going on?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. There have been mopping up going on. However, without the residents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I'd like the witness to take a look at P1775, please. This is a Javnost Article dated the 27th of February, 1993. Sir, there are two photos on the page in the B/C/S original you're going to be shown. These are the same photos I showed you on Sunday, although when I showed you them on Sunday, there was no text, it was just the photos. Could you tell me who you recognise in those pictures, in those photos?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: I can recognise Veljko Milankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have it put did -- is it on the ELMO or not? No. Let's start from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you point him out, please.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: [indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And in the other photo -- well it's obvious.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: This and this is Veljko Milankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Is there any -- is that the same man you saw giving orders at the sawmill?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I'd like to show the witness now a document which does not have an exhibit number. It's been listed. It's disclosure number 4.631, English ERN number is 0110-3705. It's the 5th of June, command of the 1st Krajina Corps, order. It has been provided.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Excuse me, since it does not have a document number, can I see a copy of it as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's got 4.631 on the top right, it's probably the only -- we have an extra copy if you need one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It was distributed this morning, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Yes, okay, I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think it was earlier -- oh, this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The witness doesn't have it yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, this order in paragraph 2 states: "I appoint Lieutenant Veljko Milankovic as battalion commander who will carry out and receive all orders from the commander of the 327th Motorised Brigade." And it is signed by Major General Momir Talic. Is that what you have in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: My question is about paragraph 2, during the time that you saw Veljko Milankovic, what did his relationship appear to you to be to the regular VRS armed forces, at the sawmill or later, if you saw him again?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: I saw him there with a senior officer. I remember him talking to the officer and asking for a recoilless gun from him, and the officer consented to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. That will be P1802. Only one more document I want to show you, sir. This one also does not have an exhibit number. It's on our list, it's disclosure number 4.2128, it's a 1 KK document dated 23rd of June, 1993, a request for action. And if you look at point 5 of this request for action, to the main staff of the Republika Srpska -- of the army of the RS, it's a request for the proposal of decoration of several people, including Veljko Milankovic. Now, given what we talked about, the activities of Veljko Milankovic, as early as 1991, what you personally saw him do, what do you think of this order requesting that he be decorated for his services?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC
utterances.text: It is natural that they wanted Veljko to be decorated, because he did many bad things. That's why he was decorated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to move on to a large last topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That will be tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. And I'll try to finish very early tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. This last document you referred the witness to, is it -- are you tendering it as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, P1803.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: May I have the night so I can come back and comment on it? I don't know what Mr. Ackerman has had before or what notice he had of that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's been disclosed. It's on our list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's disclosed today obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's been disclosed. I don't know what time but it has been disclosed a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will reconvene tomorrow, 9.00. Ms. Chuqing can I have the timetable for Thursday so that I will announce the hours that we are sitting. Thursday, we will be starting at 9.00 in the morning. We start at 9.00 in the morning and we finish the morning sitting at 12.30. Then we will reconvene at 2.00 and finish at 4.00. And that basically means we will gain an hour a day while we sit. These hours, we will be gaining one hour's hearing time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 1.45 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 21st day of May, 2003, at 9.00 a.m.
